snake_plant.name_note: Formerly Sansevieria trifasciata. Also called mother-in-law's tongue; in Tagalog tigre or buntot-tigre (buntot-tigre is also used for Sansevieria roxburghiana).

note.text: Snake plants are kept in many classrooms to freshen the air, but a 2020 review of 12 chamber studies found that one potted plant removes very little indoor pollution: matching ordinary ventilation would take 10 to 1,000 plants per square metre of floor. Open windows and fans matter far more. The leaves are mildly toxic if eaten (vomiting, nausea), and the sap can irritate skin, so keep it away from small children and pets. It has few pests and diseases; watch for mealybugs and spider mites.

conditions.name: Black rot
conditions.symptoms: Purple flecks on leaves that become round spots with brown centers and purple edges ('frogeye'). Fruit gets firm brown rot with black and brown rings and may shrivel into mummies that stay on the tree.
look_for: Round leaf spots with brown centers and purple edges?
Shriveled, mummified fruit still on the tree?
management: Remove dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit; bury the prunings or seal them in a bag (open burning of farm waste is banned in the Philippines).
Plant disease-free seedlings in well-drained soil.

conditions.name: Apple mosaic
conditions.symptoms: Cream to yellow spots, blotches, bands or vein patterns on the upper side of leaves; yield loss is usually slight.
look_for: Bright cream or yellow patterns on the leaves?
Fruit looks normal?
management: Buy virus-tested trees from reputable nurseries.
Do not take graftwood from infected trees.
No chemical treatment works; remove badly affected trees if needed.

conditions.name: Cedar apple rust
conditions.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf with tiny black dots in the center and a red band around them; later, small cup-like structures form under the leaf. The fungus needs nearby cedar (juniper) trees.
look_for: Bright orange-yellow spots with tiny black dots?
Cedar or juniper trees growing nearby?
management: Plant resistant varieties.
Avoid planting near cedar trees, or remove nearby cedars.
Plant clean seedlings from reliable sources.

conditions.name: Apple scab
conditions.symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots with uneven edges on leaves and fruit; fruit spots become dark, rough and corky, and badly infected leaves yellow and drop.
look_for: Olive-green velvety spots on leaves?
Dark, rough, corky spots on the fruit?
management: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves.
Prune to keep an open canopy and space trees properly.
Plant disease-free seedlings from certified nurseries.

conditions.name: Anthracnose
conditions.symptoms: Brown to black spots on the fruit peel that grow into large dark sunken areas, especially on ripening fruit.
look_for: Dark sunken spots on the fruit peel?
Spots growing as the fruit ripens?
management: Avoid injuring the fruit during harvest and handling.
Remove old flower parts that can carry the fungus.

conditions.name: Black leaf streak (black Sigatoka)
conditions.symptoms: Small red-brown streaks along the veins on young leaves that become dark spots with gray centers, black edges and yellow halos; large parts of the leaf die and bunches ripen unevenly.
look_for: Red-brown streaks running along the leaf veins?
Dark spots with yellow halos on older leaves?
management: Plant disease-free, tolerant planting material.
Space plants, control weeds and remove extra suckers so leaves dry quickly.
Remove leaves with mature spots.
Act as soon as the first symptoms appear, especially in humid weather.

conditions.name: Bunchy top
conditions.symptoms: Each new leaf is smaller and stands upright in a bunch at the top; leaf edges are pale and wavy, with dark-green 'dot-dash' streaks along the veins. Spread by aphids.
look_for: New leaves small and bunched upright at the top?
Dark-green dot-dash streaks along the veins?
management: Use disease-free planting material from a registered nursery.
Do not bring planting material from affected areas.
Control aphids and keep fields weed-free.
Uproot and destroy infected plants.

ph.text: PCAARRD calls bunchy top the most destructive banana virus disease in the country. There is no cure. The banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) spreads it, and Lakatan, the most popular local dessert banana, is affected.
steps: Replant with tissue-cultured plantlets.
Keep the mat clean: weed, remove old leaves and extra suckers, and fertilize based on a soil test.

conditions.name: Cigar end rot
conditions.symptoms: The tips of the fingers darken, wrinkle and rot; the rotted tip may dry out or be covered with gray-white spores, like the ash of a cigar.
look_for: Finger tips dark and rotted?
Gray, ash-like covering on the rotted tips?
management: Remove dead flower parts from the bunch.
Cover bunches with perforated plastic bags.

conditions.name: Cordana leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Oval pale brown spots near the leaf edges on lower leaves, with rings inside and a yellow halo; spots can merge into large dead areas.
look_for: Oval brown spots near the leaf edge?
Rings inside the spots with a yellow halo?
management: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
If severe, ask a technician about a copper-based fungicide.

conditions.name: Panama disease (Fusarium wilt)
conditions.name_note: Forma specialis of Fusarium oxysporum; GBIF does not list formae speciales separately.
conditions.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow and wilt, leaf sheaths split and the whole canopy dies. Inside the pseudostem and rhizome, the vascular tissue is reddish brown.
look_for: Older leaves yellowing and wilting from the edges?
Reddish-brown streaks inside when the pseudostem is cut?
management: There is no cure once a plant is infected.
Plant only disease-free planting material.
The fungus spreads in soil, running water and infected rhizomes, so keep these from moving out of infected areas.

sources.title: Mnyauko fusari (Fusarium wilt or Panama disease) wa migomba

ph.text: The tropical race 4 (TR4) strain affected about 15,500 hectares in Davao Region in 2025, according to DA. In Davao trials, the resistant Cavendish clones GCTCV 218 (moderate resistance, good bunches) and GCTCV 219 (high resistance, but with malformed hands) were tested; resistance changed from site to site.
steps: Disinfect footwear and tires when leaving an affected farm (the BPI order requires foot and tire baths).
Cavendish growers: ask DA or BPI about the resistant clones GCTCV 218 and 219.
ph.regulated: Rules apply. A 2012 BPI order bans moving banana and abaca plants, plant parts, soil and packing material out of infected provinces (the Davao provinces, Bukidnon, North and South Cotabato, and areas declared later); tissue-cultured plants are exempt. Do not move suckers, soil or leaves from an affected farm, and report the case to your DA regional office or BPI. The order is from 2012, so ask BPI for the current list of areas.

conditions.name: Downy mildew
conditions.symptoms: Leaves yellow, often starting along the middle vein, with gray fuzzy growth underneath; brown-black angular patches follow.
look_for: Gray fuzzy growth under the leaves?
Yellowing that starts along the middle vein?
management: Grow tolerant varieties.
Keep air moving around plants and water with drip lines to keep leaves dry.

conditions.name: Halo blight
conditions.name_note: Pathovar name used in plant pathology; GBIF does not list pathovars separately.
conditions.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots under the leaf that turn brown, surrounded by a wide yellow-green halo; pods get red-brown greasy spots.
look_for: Wide yellow halo around small brown spots?
Greasy spots on the pods?
management: Plant disease-free seed.
Rotate to non-host crops every two years and plow bean debris under.

conditions.name: Bean common mosaic
conditions.symptoms: Light and dark green mottling, downward curling or cupping of leaves, and deformed pods; plants from infected seed are stunted. Spread by seed and aphids.
look_for: Mottled leaves that curl down or cup?
Stunted plants with misshapen pods?
management: Use certified disease-free seed.
Plant resistant varieties.
Controlling aphids may slow spread; there is no chemical cure.

conditions.name: Bean rust
conditions.symptoms: Small yellow-white spots that become raised brick-red pustules, often with a yellow halo; leaves may drop early.
look_for: Raised brick-red pustules?
Reddish powder that rubs off?
management: Grow resistant varieties.
Remove infected debris, rotate crops and control weeds.

conditions.name: Bacterial spot
conditions.symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaf undersides that dry and turn brown; raised brown cankers on stems and cracked brown spots on fruit.
look_for: Water-soaked spots that turn brown?
Rough, cracked spots on the fruit?
management: Use disease-free seed and transplants.
Remove crop debris after harvest or plow it deeply under.

conditions.name: Blossom end rot
conditions.symptoms: A water-soaked spot at the blossom end of the fruit that becomes sunken, tan and leathery. It is not an infection: it comes from low calcium in the fruit, often caused by uneven watering.
look_for: Sunken leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of the fruit?
Leaves otherwise healthy?
management: Water evenly and mulch to keep soil moisture steady.
Keep soil pH near 6.5; lime if needed.
Avoid ammonium fertilizers and over-fertilizing.

conditions.name: Frogeye leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small round spots with white to brown centers and a dark red-purple border, like a frog's eye; old spots crack in the middle.
look_for: Round spots with light centers and dark borders?
Spot centers brittle or cracked?
management: Remove crop debris after harvest.
Rotate crops.

conditions.name: Powdery mildew
conditions.symptoms: White powdery patches on the underside of leaves with yellow to brown areas on top; leaf edges curl up and leaves may drop.
look_for: White powder under the leaves?
Yellow patches on the upper side?
management: Ask a technician about a fungicide if the disease is severe.

conditions.name: Anthracnose
conditions.symptoms: Usually hidden until ripening: ripe berries soften and shrivel near the blossom end and ooze small orange spore masses. Twig blight and leaf spots can also occur.
look_for: Ripe berries soft and shriveled at the blossom end?
Orange, slimy spore masses on the fruit?
management: Plant less susceptible varieties.
Prune for air flow and shorten leaf wetness with drip irrigation.
Cool and handle harvested fruit quickly.

conditions.name: Botrytis blight (gray mold)
conditions.symptoms: Open blossoms turn brown and blighted and do not set fruit; leaves touching infected blossoms get brown spots. Gray mold may cover affected parts.
look_for: Brown, blighted blossoms?
Gray fuzzy mold on flowers or fruit?
management: Protect flowers at mid-bloom and late bloom when the disease is a problem.

conditions.name: Mummy berry
conditions.symptoms: New shoots and leaves suddenly droop and brown in spring; infected berries turn cream or pink, then tan or gray, and shrivel into hard mummies.
look_for: New shoots wilting and browning in spring?
Berries shriveled into hard, gray mummies?
management: Plant disease-free plants.
Remove mummified berries or bury them under at least 2.5 cm of soil.

conditions.name: Leaf rust
conditions.name_note: Formerly Thekopsora minima (NSW DPI); Pucciniastrum vaccinii in western North America.
conditions.symptoms: Small angular yellow spots on the upper leaf that turn red to black, with yellow-orange powdery pustules underneath; badly infected bushes lose leaves early. Worse near hemlock trees.
look_for: Yellow-orange powder under the leaves?
Yellow spots turning red-brown on top?
management: Choose more resistant varieties.
Scout regularly and remove nearby hemlocks where practical.

conditions.name: Blueberry scorch
conditions.symptoms: Flowers and leaves suddenly die and blight in spring on sensitive varieties; other varieties show no symptoms. Spread by aphids and takes 1-2 years to show.
look_for: Flowers and new leaves dying suddenly at bloom?
Whole bush or branches affected, not single leaves?
management: Plant virus-tested stock and test bushes with symptoms.
Remove and destroy infected plants and control aphids.
Clean harvesting equipment.

conditions.name: Alternaria leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small dark spots that turn brown to gray, often with rings and a purple-black edge; the centers can crack. Dark streaks may form on stems.
look_for: Brown-gray spots with rings?
Dark purple-black edge around the spots?
management: Plant only clean seed.
Rotate away from cabbage-family crops.

conditions.name: Downy mildew

conditions.symptoms: Small angular yellow patches on the upper leaf that turn brown, with white fluffy growth underneath.
look_for: White fluffy growth under the leaf?
Angular yellow patches on top?
management: Remove crop debris after harvest.
Rotate with non-cabbage-family crops.

conditions.name: Ring spot
conditions.symptoms: Small purple spots with a water-soaked ring that become brown spots 1-2 cm across with olive-green borders, often with rings of tiny black dots.
look_for: Round brown spots with many tiny black dots in rings?
Olive-green border around the spots?
management: Avoid fields that had the disease before.
Rotate with non-cabbage-family crops and clean tools regularly.

conditions.name: Alternaria leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small dark spots that turn brown to gray, often with rings and a purple-black edge; the centers can crack.
look_for: Brown-gray spots with rings?
Dark purple-black edge around the spots?
management: Plant only clean seed.
Rotate away from cabbage-family crops.

conditions.name: Black rot
conditions.symptoms: Yellow to brown V-shaped patches that start at the leaf edge and point toward the midrib; veins and stems turn black.
look_for: V-shaped yellow-brown patches starting at the leaf edge?
Blackened veins?
management: Plant clean seed and resistant varieties.
Rotate away from cabbage-family crops for two years.
Remove cabbage-family weeds and keep the field clean.

conditions.name: Downy mildew
conditions.gbif: Hyaloperonospora brassicae (Gäum.) Göker, Voglmayr, Riethm., Weiss & Oberw.
conditions.symptoms: Irregular yellow patches on leaves that turn light brown, with fluffy gray growth underneath.
look_for: Fluffy gray growth under the leaf?
Yellow patches on top of the leaf?

Rotate with non-cabbage-family crops.

conditions.name: Alternaria leaf blight
conditions.symptoms: Green-brown water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black and merge, so leaves yellow and die.
look_for: Dark brown to black spots on leaf edges?
Leaves dying from the tips?
management: Treat seed with hot water before planting.
Act early in warm, wet weather.

conditions.name: Cavity spot
conditions.name_note: GBIF accepts Globisporangium violae; older literature uses Pythium violae.
conditions.gbif: Globisporangium violae (Chesters & Hickman) Uzuhashi, Tojo & Kakish.
conditions.symptoms: Sunken, oval gray spots across the root; the skin breaks and dark elongated lesions with small cracks form.
look_for: Small sunken oval spots across the root?
Leaves look normal?
management: Avoid fields where cavity spot occurred before.
Do not over-fertilize.

conditions.name: Cercospora leaf blight
conditions.symptoms: Small dead flecks with yellow halos that grow into tan-brown spots; leaves wither, curl and die.
look_for: Small tan spots with yellow halos?
Leaves curling and drying?
management: Plant clean seed and rotate crops.
Plow crop debris under after harvest.

conditions.name: Alternaria leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small dark spots that turn brown to gray, often with rings and a purple-black edge; the centers can crack.
look_for: Brown-gray spots with rings?
Dark purple-black edge around the spots?
management: Plant only clean seed.
Rotate away from cabbage-family crops.

conditions.name: Bacterial soft rot
conditions.symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaves and curds that grow into a soft, rotten mass oozing slimy liquid that darkens in air.
look_for: Soft, slimy rot?
Bad smell from the rotting area?
management: No chemical treatment works; rely on good practices.
Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds and rotate crops.
Harvest heads only when dry and avoid damaging them.

conditions.name: Anthracnose (leaf curl)
conditions.symptoms: Leaves cup downward (leaf curl) and stay pale green; stalks get brown lesions and crowns may rot. Spread by splashing water in long wet, warm periods.
look_for: Leaves cupping downward?
Brown lesions on the stalks?
management: Hot-water treat seed and clean transplant trays.
Scout regularly and remove suspect plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation and control weed hosts.

conditions.name: Early blight
conditions.symptoms: Small yellow flecks that grow into brown-gray papery spots without clear borders; heavily spotted leaves die.
look_for: Brown-gray papery spots?
Spots without a clear border?
management: Plant clean seed and tolerant varieties.
Rotate crops and avoid crowding plants.

conditions.name: Cherry leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small purple or red spots on the upper leaf that turn brown; infected leaves yellow and drop early, weakening the tree.
look_for: Many small purple-red spots on the leaves?
Leaves yellowing and dropping in mid-season?
management: Rake and destroy fallen leaves to reduce spring infection.
Protect new leaves from petal fall on trees with a history of the disease.

conditions.name: Powdery mildew
conditions.name_note: Recently renamed Podosphaera cerasi; P. clandestina is still widely used (WSU).
conditions.symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves and shoots; leaves curl upward and new leaves stay pale and distorted. Fruit can be deformed.
look_for: White powder on leaves and young shoots?
Leaves curling upward?
management: Prune for air flow and remove infected water sprouts.
Plant resistant varieties; protect from petal fall in high-risk years.

conditions.name: Citrus canker
conditions.name_note: Marked doubtful in GBIF; this is the name used in current citrus canker literature.
conditions.symptoms: Raised corky spots with yellow halos on leaves (often at the edge or tip), twigs and fruit; old spots collapse into brown craters.
look_for: Raised, rough spots with yellow halos?
Spots on both leaves and fruit?
management: Where the disease is new, remove and destroy infected trees.
Use windbreaks and control leaf miners.
Copper sprays help where the disease is established.

conditions.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening)
conditions.name_note: Candidatus (not yet cultured) bacteria are not in the GBIF backbone.
conditions.symptoms: Blotchy yellow mottling that is not the same on both sides of the leaf vein, yellow shoots on one limb, and twig dieback. Fruit is small, lopsided, partly green and bitter. Spread by the citrus psyllid.
look_for: Blotchy yellow mottling not matching on both sides of the midrib?
Small lopsided fruit that stays partly green?
management: There is no cure; infected trees must be removed.
Plant only disease-free seedlings from a certified nursery.
Remove other host plants of the citrus psyllid near the farm and space trees well.
Follow quarantine rules on moving citrus plants.

ph.text: Found on calamansi in the Philippines: in Oriental Mindoro, 150 of 155 calamansi plants tested positive for huanglongbing, and almost all also had citrus tristeza virus. The symptoms look like zinc deficiency (blotchy yellow mottling between the veins, small thick leaves), so a lab test is needed to confirm it.
ph.regulated: Rules apply. BPI plant quarantine has restricted moving citrus planting material between provinces because of huanglongbing (for example into Negros Occidental in 2015; lab-grown material with a permit was allowed). Buy planting material from BPI, and do not bring in cuttings from other provinces.

look_for: Brown sunken spots on green berries?
Round leaf spots with gray-white centers?
management: Fertilize adequately; weak plants are more susceptible.
Remove debris after pruning.
Space and prune plants to open the canopy.

look_for: Thread-like white or light growth on twigs and leaf undersides?
Blackened dead leaves hanging from threads?
management: Prune affected branches about 30 cm below the affected part.
Combine cultural, biological and chemical measures as advised locally.

conditions.name_note: GBIF lists it under Cercosporina; plant pathology literature uses Cercospora coffeicola. Expert check advised.
conditions.symptoms: Round brown leaf spots that develop gray-white centers with a red-brown edge, like an eye, sometimes with a yellow halo; leaves may drop early.
look_for: Round spots with gray-white centers and red-brown edges?
Leaves dropping early?
management: Fertilize adequately; weak plants are more susceptible.
Remove debris after pruning.
Space and prune plants to open the canopy.

conditions.name: Coffee leaf rust
conditions.symptoms: Pale yellow spots on top of the leaf with powdery orange-yellow patches underneath, starting on lower leaves; infected leaves drop and branches go bare.
look_for: Orange-yellow powder under the leaf?
Pale yellow spots on top?
management: Plant resistant varieties.
Windbreak and shade trees can reduce the spores reaching the plants.
Copper fungicides are among the most effective and affordable controls.

Spots limited by the leaf veins?

Rotate away from corn and plow residue under.

Spots crossing the leaf veins?

Rotate with non-host crops and manage crop debris.

Rusty powder that rubs off on your finger?

Fungicides help most when there are only a few pustules per leaf.

conditions.symptoms: Swollen white to silvery galls on ears, tassels, stalks or leaves that fill with black powdery spores.
look_for: Swollen whitish galls (tumors) on the ear or tassel?
Black powder inside the galls?
management: Grow resistant or tolerant varieties and plant clean seed.
Rotate with non-cereal crops and plow deep to bury spores.
Cut out and destroy galls before they burst; do not feed infected material to livestock.

conditions.name: Angular leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that spread between the veins and become angular; in humid weather they ooze a milky liquid that dries into a white crust. Spot centers may fall out, leaving holes.

White crust or holes in the spots?
management: Use disease-free seed and resistant varieties.
Do not plant where cucurbits grew in the last two years.

conditions.symptoms: Single runners or whole plants wilt and die quickly while leaves are still dark green. Spread by cucumber beetles.
look_for: Sudden wilting of whole runners?
Cucumber beetles on the plants?
management: Control cucumber beetles; hand-pick and destroy adults.

Leaves yellowing under the powder?
management: Grow resistant varieties.

conditions.name: Cercospora leaf spot
conditions.symptoms: Small round yellowish spots on lower leaves that develop brown centers and sometimes rings; badly affected leaves dry, curl and drop.
look_for: Round spots with brown centers starting on lower leaves?
Leaves curling and dropping?

ph.text: PhilRice names blast as one of the four major rice diseases in the Philippines. It attacks the leaves, the nodes and the neck of the panicle (neck blast), and it is worse in the rainy season. PhilRice says water shortage together with humid, cool nights makes it worse. Brown spot can look like blast: brown spot lesions are solid dark brown and are common in potassium-poor soils. In PalayCheck, neck blast on more than 10% of the field, or leaf blast on more than 20% of the seedbed, means a significant yield loss.
steps: Flood the field when you can; avoid letting it dry out.
Sow clean seed early; water seeding is better than drill seeding.
Avoid too much nitrogen, and stay out of the field while plants are wet.
Destroy infected straw and stubble without burning it in the open (open burning of farm waste is banned under RA 9003).
Ask your DA office or PhilRice which blast-resistant variety suits your area (PhilRice named PSB Rc10 in 2016).

ph.text: One of PhilRice's four major rice diseases. It makes oval gray spots with black-brown edges on the leaf sheath, with hard fungal bodies (sclerotia) in severe cases. It is favoured by 28 to 32 °C, very humid air, light rain, too much nitrogen and close spacing. PhilRice warned in 2024 that it is a concern in irrigated fields of Western Visayas and can cut yield by up to 25% if left alone. In PalayCheck, more than 40% of the field affected at mid to maximum tillering means a significant yield loss.
steps: Drain the field for a few days at maximum tillering.
Split the nitrogen fertilizer into several applications, and use the recommended seeding rate.
After harvest, plow under the dry infected stubble.

conditions.symptoms: Spikelets turn bleached, light straw or white during flowering; kernels shrivel and discolor, and pink or dark purple-black bodies may form on the spike.
look_for: Bleached spikelets in an otherwise green head?
Shriveled, discolored kernels?
management: Plant certified clean seed and tolerant varieties.
Rotate with legumes and choose well-drained sites.
Scout at flowering when humidity is high.

conditions.name: Leaf rust
conditions.name_note: GBIF lumps it into P. recondita; wheat literature uses P. triticina for leaf rust.
conditions.symptoms: Small round orange-brown pustules scattered on the leaf blades and sheaths; spores rub off on your finger. Pustules turn dark near maturity.
look_for: Small scattered orange-brown pustules?
Orange powder that rubs off on your finger?
management: Plant resistant varieties, the best control; check current ratings, since resistance can break down.
Remove volunteer wheat and crop debris.
Avoid very early sowing and excess nitrogen.

conditions.name: Loose smut
conditions.symptoms: At heading, the spikelets are replaced by black, sooty spore masses and no grain forms.
look_for: Black, sooty heads instead of grain?
Only some heads in the field affected?
management: Plant certified, treated seed; the fungus lives inside the seed.
Grow resistant cultivars.

conditions.name: Powdery mildew
conditions.name_note: Forma specialis of Blumeria graminis.
conditions.symptoms: White cottony patches on the upper side of lower leaves that turn gray-brown, later with black specks; fields can look yellowish.
look_for: White cottony patches on the leaves?
Mostly on the lower leaves at first?
management: Plant resistant varieties.
Avoid heavy nitrogen and very high seeding rates that make dense canopies.

conditions.name: Septoria tritici blotch
conditions.gbif: Zymoseptoria tritici (Roberge ex Desm.) Quaedvl. & Crous
conditions.symptoms: Pale gray to dark brown blotches on leaves with tiny black dots inside, starting on the lower leaves.
look_for: Brown blotches with tiny black dots?
Starting on the lower leaves?
management: Plant tolerant varieties and disease-free seed.
Rotate with legumes for at least a year and plow deep before planting.

conditions.name: Stem rust
conditions.name_note: Forma specialis of Puccinia graminis.
conditions.gbif: Puccinia graminis subsp. tritici A.L.Guyot, Massenot & Saccas, 1946
conditions.symptoms: Reddish-brown, powdery, elongated blister-like pustules on stems, leaves and glumes; they turn black late in the season.
look_for: Long reddish-brown pustules on the stems?
Pustules that break through both leaf sides?
management: Plant resistant varieties and certified seed; plant early.
Remove volunteer wheat and grass weeds that host the rust.
Inspect every 7-10 days from flag leaf to grain fill.

conditions.name: Stripe rust
conditions.name_note: Forma specialis of Puccinia striiformis.
conditions.symptoms: Yellow stripes of powdery spores (like turmeric powder) running along the leaves, especially the flag leaf.
look_for: Yellow powdery stripes along the leaf?
Powder that rubs off like turmeric?
management: Sow resistant varieties on time and use balanced fertilizer.
Monitor closely during dewy weather and in waterlogged areas.

conditions.name: Bacterial wilt
conditions.symptoms: Vines wilt badly and die quickly while leaves stay dark green; dark streaks may appear on leaves and stems. Spread by cucumber beetles.
look_for: Sudden severe wilting of vines?
Cucumber beetles on the plants?
management: Control cucumber beetles; hand-pick and destroy adults.

ph.text: LeafScan's research found no Philippine record of this beetle-spread bacterium (Erwinia tracheiphila). In Philippine surveys, the common bacterial wilt of vegetables is caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, on tomato, pepper, eggplant and ampalaya. A plant clinic can tell which one it is.

conditions.symptoms: White powdery growth on the upper side of leaves and on stems; affected parts are stunted and distorted.

Mostly on the upper leaf surface?
management: Plant in sunny sites with good air flow and do not crowd plants.

conditions.name: Zucchini yellow mosaic
conditions.symptoms: Plants are badly stunted; leaves show yellow mosaic, blistering and deformation, and fruits are misshapen. Spread by aphids.
look_for: Yellow mosaic and blistered leaves?
Knobby, misshapen fruit?
management: Use resistant varieties, the most effective control.
Aphid sprays rarely stop the virus.

ph.text: On kalabasa (squash) in the Philippines, mosaic and leaf-curl symptoms usually come from a mix of viruses. Squash leaf curl virus, spread by whiteflies, was found in 67% of squash across 24 provinces, often together with zucchini yellow mosaic, papaya ringspot (type W) and cucumber mosaic viruses, which aphids spread, and cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus. A photo cannot tell which virus it is. DA calls mosaic the most damaging squash disease. Spread through seed has not been reported for the Philippine squash leaf curl virus.
steps: Pull out infected plants early, and bury them or seal them in a bag; do not burn them in the open.
Keep whiteflies and aphids down, and remove weeds around the field.
Plant a virus-tolerant squash variety (DA's 2017 guide lists Suprema F1).

more.about: Plants that looked healthy suddenly wilt and die; the bacteria live in the soil. A 2017 survey found it the most common and serious vegetable disease in Eastern Visayas, on tomato, pepper, eggplant and ampalaya, and DA ranks it with Fusarium wilt as the most destructive eggplant diseases. A leaf photo cannot show it: look at the whole plant. A plant clinic can tell bacterial wilt from Fusarium wilt.
steps: Uproot wilted plants with their roots, and bury them or seal them in a bag away from the field; do not burn them in the open.
Rotate crops. The Tagalog ampalaya guide warns against planting where bacterial wilt hit eggplant, tomato or pepper before.
Plant a resistant variety: IPB-UPLB's 'Mamburao' eggplant was observed resistant (2012), and the ATI guide lists A 300 and Mara.
For tomato, grafting onto eggplant rootstock helped plants survive wet-season flooding and bacterial wilt in Philippine on-farm trials.
Homemade plant sprays will not help: no plant extract stopped this bacterium in Philippine lab tests.

more.about: Plants make mostly male flowers (hence the name, from "barako"), the leaves become thick, vein-banded and shiny, and plants are stunted. It was first seen around 1996 in La Union, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Quezon and Cavite. A 2003 report called the cause unknown (boron with plastic mulch gave partial recovery); later UPLB work (2008) linked it to cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus, spread by the cotton aphid (apaya). The name belongs to ampalaya, not to squash mosaic.
steps: Keep aphids (apaya) down.

more.about: One of PhilRice's four major rice diseases, common in irrigated and rainfed rice, especially in the wet season. Seedlings wilt (kresek); leaf blades and tips get water-soaked, then yellow-orange stripes, with yellow-orange bacterial ooze. It is favoured by too much nitrogen, lack of phosphorus and potassium, and warm, humid, rainy weather. In PalayCheck, more than 30% of the field with blight on the flag leaf at maturity means a significant loss. PhilRice says spraying chemicals against it is not economical or effective.
steps: When you see it: drain the field and keep the soil just saturated, and hold back nitrogen.
Keep seedbeds and fields from flooding, with 2 to 3 cm of water.
Use clean seed of a resistant variety, handle seedlings gently at transplanting, and remove weed hosts.
After harvest, plow under the dry infected stubble and let the field dry (fallow).

more.about: One of PhilRice's four major rice diseases, spread by the green leafhopper from seedling to tillering stage. Young leaves are mottled, older leaves turn yellow to yellow-orange, and plants are stunted with slightly fewer tillers. Late or out-of-step planting makes it worse. Nitrogen deficiency looks similar, but then the whole plant is evenly yellowish green; zinc deficiency gives dusty brown spots on upper leaves of stunted plants 2 to 4 weeks after transplanting.
steps: Uproot infected plants as soon as you see them, and bury them.
Plant a resistant variety; PhilRice lists varieties resistant to the green leafhopper.
Plant at the same time as neighbouring farms, and leave the field fallow for at least a month between crops.
Destroy the stubble after harvest.

more.about: Historically the most damaging corn disease in the Philippines, first reported in 1916, with farm losses of 15 to 40% and sometimes 80 to 95%. White-yellow stripes start at the leaf base and spread over the leaf, with whitish growth when the air is humid; plants are stunted and ears and tassels form poorly. The spores need dew or a film of water on the leaves and very humid nights.
steps: Plant a downy-mildew-resistant variety.
Pull out infected plants (rogueing) and destroy alternate hosts.
Time planting for when the disease is lowest in your area.

more.about: Common on corn in Mindanao. About 25 to 30 days after planting, the lowest leaf sheaths get irregular brownish patches with reddish-brown edges that form bands and later turn dirty white; small dark-brown fungal bodies (sclerotia) form on dead tissue. It can reach the leaves, stalk and ear.
steps: Plow deep to bury the sclerotia.
Avoid varieties whose ears are set low on the stalk.
Strip the leaves above the affected part and below the ear shoot.

more.about: Bugtok discolours the fruit pulp and is very common in cooking bananas (Saba, Cardaba); Moko is the wilt seen mostly on Cavendish. Insects carry the bacteria to the flowers, and dirty cutting tools and infected planting material spread it too. Fusarium wilt (Panama disease) also wilts bananas; a plant clinic can tell them apart.
steps: Disinfect tools used for removing suckers, buds and leaves.
Use disease-free planting material, and remove weeds and volunteer plants.
Find and remove infected plants early; bury them or seal them in a bag instead of burning them in the open.
Bag the flowers early, and on tall cooking bananas remove the male bud as soon as the false hands appear.

more.about: Most common on Saba and Cardaba, but Cavendish can get it too. Mosaic patterns, discoloured streaks on the bract, pseudostem and leaves; severe infection can stop flowering, with 40 to 70% yield loss. A survey found it in 45 to 100% of plants in more than 20 provinces. The banana aphid spreads it. There is no chemical control.
steps: Use virus-free planting material where you can get it (it is still scarce); ask your DA office or UPLB.

more.about: One of the main mango diseases, with blossom blight, scab and stem-end rot (PCAARRD). In a UPLB trial on 'Carabao' mango, all unbagged rainy-season fruit that was not hot-water treated got anthracnose.
steps: Bag the fruit with brown paper or newsprint about 2 months after flower induction.
After harvest, dip the fruit in hot water at 53 °C for 10 minutes; with bagging, this cut anthracnose by 83% in the UPLB trial.

more.about: Yellow spotting of the leaves and stunting, then early decline and death of the palm. Contaminated harvesting scythes, bolos and knives can spread it; no insect carrier is known. It also infects anahaw, buri and oil palm. There is no cure: infected palms are replaced.
